title: Did God Choose Me, or Did I Choose God?
excerpt: Christians have argued for sixteen centuries over whether God chooses who will be saved or people freely choose him, and the churches that disagree about it still confess the same gospel.
body:
Two kinds of people lose sleep over this question. The first has heard that God chose his people before the world began, and lies awake wondering whether she is one of them. She has prayed, and she believes as well as she knows how. But if the decision was made before she was born, how would she ever know which way it went? The second has heard that it all comes down to his own free choice, and he wonders whether he chose hard enough. He walked an aisle at fourteen and again at nineteen. He isn't sure either one took. If his salvation rests on the quality of his own decision, then it rests on the least reliable thing he knows.

There is a third person in the room, and she is usually the angriest. Her son has walked away from the faith. One friend tells her that God is sovereign and her son is in his hands. Another tells her that God is a gentleman who never forces anyone. She can't tell which of those is supposed to be the comfort.

Most arguments about predestination happen a long way from these three. Each side learns to describe the other in a sentence the other would never sign. The Calvinist is told he worships a tyrant who makes puppets. The Arminian is told he worships his own willpower. Both are slanders. The argument is far older than Calvin, and its history is more careful than our tempers.

## Augustine and Pelagius

Near the end of the fourth century, Augustine, a bishop in North Africa, wrote the story of his own conversion in a book called the *Confessions*. In it he prays a line that he repeats several times: "Give what Thou commandest, and command what Thou wilt." He meant that he could not obey God unless God first gave him the power to obey.

A British teacher in Rome named Pelagius heard that prayer quoted and was appalled. Pelagius had a serious case. Rome was full of baptized people who lived exactly as they had lived before, and who excused themselves by saying that human nature is weak. Pelagius thought Augustine's prayer handed them their excuse. A just God, he reasoned, doesn't command what a person is unable to do. If God says "be holy," then holiness must be within reach, and telling people otherwise is how you get a lazy church.

Augustine answered that Pelagius had the patient wrong. The human will isn't a neutral thing, standing between good and evil and free to pick. It is bent. We do what we want, and that is the trouble, because what we want has gone wrong at the root. A person in that condition doesn't need better instructions. He needs a new heart, and nobody gives himself one.

Pelagius's follower Caelestius was condemned by a council at Carthage in 411. A larger council there condemned the teaching in 418, and the Council of Ephesus did the same in 431. The church had decided that we don't save ourselves. It had not decided everything Augustine went on to say. In his last years he pressed the logic further: if faith itself is God's gift, then God gives it to some and not to others, and he chose which before they were born. Many who had stood with him against Pelagius couldn't follow him there. Monks in southern Gaul, serious and devout men, replied that surely the first small turn toward God, the wanting to be healed, belongs to us, and grace meets it.

In 529 a small council of bishops met at Orange, in what is now southern France, to settle that quarrel. What they wrote is worth more attention than it gets, because both sides of the modern argument can claim it. Against the monks, they said that even the first desire for God is his gift: "The sin of the first man has so impaired and weakened free will that no one thereafter can either love God as he ought or believe in God or do good for God's sake, unless the grace of divine mercy has preceded him." Grace comes first, every time. But they refused the darkest reading of Augustine in the same breath: "We not only do not believe that any are foreordained to evil by the power of God, but even state with utter abhorrence that if there are those who want to believe so evil a thing, they are anathema." The council left unanswered why one person comes and another doesn't. The argument has gone on inside those two fences ever since.

## Luther, Erasmus, and Dort

A thousand years later the same question broke open again. In 1524 Erasmus, the most famous scholar in Europe, wrote a short book defending free will against Martin Luther. Erasmus thought the matter obscure and asked for modesty. Luther answered in 1525 with *The Bondage of the Will*, and he thanked Erasmus for one thing: of all his opponents, Erasmus alone had gone for the real issue and not for side matters like indulgences. For Luther this was the center. If any part of salvation rests on us, he argued, then no troubled conscience can ever be sure of it.

The Catholic Church gave its answer at the Council of Trent in 1547. Trent agreed with Orange that grace comes first and that no one can take a step toward God without it. It added that the will, once moved by grace, truly cooperates and is able to refuse. Catholic theologians then fell into their own dispute over how grace and freedom fit together, Dominicans against Jesuits, until 1607, when Pope Paul V ended the hearings in Rome without a ruling and forbade each side to call the other heretical.

Luther's heirs took a path of their own. In 1577 the Lutheran churches confessed that God chooses his people by grace alone, and that this is pure comfort. They declined to teach that God chooses anyone for damnation. If a person is saved, it is God's doing entirely, and if he is lost, it is his own.

Among the Reformed, the crisis came in the Netherlands. Jacobus Arminius, a Dutch pastor who became a professor at Leiden, had come to believe that God's choosing rests on his foreknowledge of who would believe, and that grace can be resisted. He died in 1609. The next year his followers set out their views in five articles, and in 1618 and 1619 a synod met at Dort, with delegates from Britain, Germany and Switzerland, and answered them point by point. That is where the famous five points come from. They were five replies to five objections, never a summary of the Christian faith.

Dort has a harsher name than its text has earned. The same canons that teach unconditional election say that the death of Christ is "abundantly sufficient to expiate the sins of the whole world," and that the promise of the gospel "ought to be declared and published to all nations, and to all persons promiscuously and without distinction."

But Dort was also a state affair, and that part ought to trouble us. When the synod ended, the Dutch government removed the Arminian ministers from their pulpits and banished many of them. Christians had settled a question about grace with the help of the police.

## Wesley and Whitefield

The argument reached the English-speaking world through two friends. John Wesley and George Whitefield had been students together at Oxford, and together they led the awakening that swept Britain and the American colonies in the 1730s and 1740s. Wesley was an Arminian. Whitefield was a Calvinist. Wesley preached and printed a sermon called *Free Grace*, attacking predestination, and Whitefield answered in a public letter: "You plainly make salvation depend not on GOD's free-grace, but on man's free-will." By 1741 the two were openly divided, and their followers said bitter things.

The friendship survived it. When Whitefield died in 1770, Wesley preached his funeral sermon in London, at Whitefield's own request. He told the crowd that there are doctrines over which sincere Christians have been divided for ages. "In these we may think and let think; we may 'agree to disagree.'" Then he named what his old opponent had preached everywhere he went. Whitefield's fundamental point, Wesley said, was to "Give God all the glory of whatever is good in man." And the Arminian went on, in his own voice, to say what the Calvinist had taught and what he taught too: "There is no power in man, till it is given him from above, to do one good work, to speak one good word, or to form one good desire."

## What the Passages Say

Romans 9 is the passage Calvinists love and Arminians are tempted to explain away. Paul is grieving that most of his own people have not believed in their Messiah, and he asks whether God's promise has failed. His answer reaches back to Jacob and Esau. Before the twins were born or had done anything good or bad, God chose the younger, "in order that God's purpose of election might continue, not because of works but because of him who calls" (Romans 9:11). Then Paul draws the conclusion: "So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy" (9:16). He expects an objection, and the objection he expects tells us what he has been saying: "Why does he still find fault? For who can resist his will?" (9:19). Nobody raises that objection against a teaching that leaves the last word with us.

But Paul's argument doesn't end at chapter 9, and the Arminian is right to keep reading. The subject of these three chapters is Israel and the nations, and how God's mercy has moved through history from one to the other. The man who wrote chapter 9 begins chapter 10 by praying for the very people he has just described: "my heart's desire and prayer to God for them is that they may be saved" (10:1). He says that "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved" (10:13). And his conclusion is wider than anything a narrow reading would predict: "For God has consigned all to disobedience, that he may have mercy on all" (11:32).

John 6 works the same way. Jesus says, "No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him" (John 6:44), and "All that the Father gives me will come to me" (6:37). The Reformed reader hears that the Father's drawing brings a person, and doesn't fail. The Arminian reader points to the same Gospel six chapters later, where Jesus uses the same verb: "And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself" (12:32). He points to the middle of the same speech, where the Father's will is "that everyone who looks on the Son and believes in him should have eternal life" (6:40).

Then there are the texts Arminians love and Calvinists must not shrink. God "desires all people to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth" (1 Timothy 2:4). The Lord is patient, "not wishing that any should perish, but that all should reach repentance" (2 Peter 3:9). Through Ezekiel God says, "I have no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn from his way and live" (Ezekiel 33:11). Reformed readers have answers. "All people" in 1 Timothy follows a call to pray for kings and every class of person. Peter says God is patient "toward you," and he is writing to the church. Those answers have force. The Reformed confessions also take these verses seriously. Dort itself says that all who are called by the gospel "are unfeignedly called," which is an old way of saying that God means the invitation.

## The Positions at Their Best

The Reformed Christian says that a dead man doesn't raise himself. If we were truly lost, then the faith that saves us had to be given, and God gave it to those he chose for reasons that lie in his mercy and not in them. Nothing about this makes people robots. The Westminster Confession says that God ordains whatever comes to pass, and yet "neither is God the author of sin, nor is violence offered to the will of the creatures." What the Reformed Christian fears in the other view is that it makes the believer's own decision the thing that separates the saved from the lost, which gives him something to boast of and leaves the anxious with nothing to stand on.

The Arminian Christian, and Wesley's heirs with him, agrees that no one can come to God unaided. Grace goes before everyone, restoring enough freedom to answer. But God wants every person, Christ died for every person, and a love that can't be refused isn't what Scripture means by love. God chooses those he foreknows will trust his Son. What the Arminian fears in the other view is a God who commands all to repent while withholding from most the ability to do it, and whose invitation to the world isn't meant.

The Lutheran affirms election, will not affirm its dark twin, and says so without embarrassment. The Catholic insists on grace first and on real cooperation after, and holds that grace can be lost. The Orthodox churches, who never took Augustine as their main teacher, speak of *synergy*, a working together in which God's grace and human freedom are not rivals.

All of them stand against Pelagius. Every one of these traditions confesses that salvation is by grace, that grace comes first, that no one will stand before God and take credit, and that God is not the author of evil. Every one of them preaches to everyone and prays for the lost. The Arminian, on her knees for her son, asks God to change his heart, which is a strangely Calvinist thing to ask. The Calvinist gets up from his knees and pleads with his neighbor as though the neighbor could say yes, which is exactly what Wesley would have told him to do.

## How Much Rides on It

Some questions the creeds settle. That God is Father, Son and Holy Spirit, that Jesus Christ is true God and true man, that he died for our sins and rose bodily: the church confesses these, and a person who denies them has left the faith. That we are saved by grace and not by our own effort belongs with them. Pelagius was not a second opinion.

How God's choosing and our believing fit together is a different kind of question. The Apostles' Creed and the Nicene Creed are silent on it. Churches that agree on everything in those creeds have divided over it for centuries and are still divided, and this essay does not settle it. It sets the positions out because faithful Christians stand on both sides, reading the same Bible and trusting the same Lord. It shapes how a church preaches, prays and comforts. It is not the gospel, and treating it as the gospel has done real harm.

We have done that harm. Some of us have held the doctrine of election like a membership card, and looked at unbelieving neighbors as though the matter were closed. Some have used it to excuse a church that never crossed the street or the ocean. On the other side, we have turned faith into a performance, measured conversions by technique, and left tender people wondering for decades whether they had been sincere enough. Each side has called the other a different religion. The Westminster divines, who taught predestination without apology, wrote that this "high mystery" is "to be handled with special prudence and care." We have often handled it like a club.

## For the One Who Is Afraid

Go back to the three people at the beginning. Nothing on either side of this argument tells the first woman to search for her name in a hidden book. Nobody has ever been given that book to read. What she has been given is a promise, spoken by the same Jesus in the same speech as the hardest words about the Father's drawing: "whoever comes to me I will never cast out" (John 6:37). Reformed and Arminian pastors say the same thing to her, and they are right to. Come. If you come, you will not be turned away.

The man who wonders whether he chose hard enough can hear what both sides also agree on: his faith is not the savior. Christ is. Weak faith in a strong Savior saves, because the strength was never in the faith.

And the mother can pray. She doesn't have to solve this first. She is asking the only one who can reach her son to reach him, and she is asking a God who has said he takes no pleasure in anyone's death.

When Paul came to the end of the three chapters, he didn't offer an explanation of how God's mercy and human unbelief had fit together. He stopped arguing and began to worship: "Oh, the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!" (Romans 11:33).

He knew less than we would like him to have told us, and he knew enough to trust the God whose mercy he couldn't map.

The church has been trying to draw that map for sixteen hundred years. The mercy is still larger than the map.

*"So then it depends not on human will or exertion, but on God, who has mercy."* (Romans 9:16)

*"For everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved."* (Romans 10:13)
